title: Sacrifices of Glory
reviewNotes: Reconstructed seven-piece position after ...Bh3. Three checked branches: bishop diversion/knight preparation, actual stalemate after premature d8=Q Re8+ Qxe8, and king-declines-sacrifice fork. Saved final board confirms the checking rook move after Nf2 is ...Rg3+, not ...Re8+, before Kh8. Earlier eight-piece setup is context.
transcript: Knight 2 e2, a brilliant sacrifice that tries to stop the black pawn from promoting. But of course, if the bishop takes the knight, now the other bishop is going to also stop the promotion, which means that white would get a new queen and win the game. But black is not that naive, and instead of taking the knight, he just promotes to a queen anyway. This doesn't seem to make sense, but actually, if we capture the queen, now black is going to be able to play rook to d3 and stop the promotion, winning the game. Which means that white's best try is to recapture the queen with the bishop, preparing to meet rook to d3 with a fork of the rook and king. It doesn't seem like black can stop the promotion to a new queen, but actually, he can with bishop to h3, attacking the pawn and preparing to meet the promotion with rook to c8, which would pin the queen to the king and land us in a drawn endgame. So actually, after bishop to h3, white has to play knight f4 check, forking the king and the bishop. Now, if the king goes down, we're just going to promote with a check. So the king goes to h6, and now after the bishop is collected, the black rook has to try and stop the pawn. And luckily, since the king is not on h5 anymore, white doesn't have a fork. The king is too far, and the bishop is going to need at least two moves to support the pawn. So is this it? Is black simply out of the woods in this position? Well, not exactly. White has the majestic bishop to e3 check, and the bishop has to be taken because if the king moves to either g6 or h5, there is still going to be the fork of the rook and king. But after the rook takes, white has to be careful one last time, because actually, promoting to a queen would be a blunder after the counter brilliancy rook to e8 check. If the rook is taken, this would actually be a stalemate, a situation where there's is checkmate, but the opponent has no [music] legal moves, so a draw. So, instead of allowing this, white has to find the incredibly precise knight to F2, threatening to fork the rook and the king, and defending the D3 square, which is the only square that the rook can use to stop the pawn. Of course, black can throw a desperate check to white king, but after king to H8, using the opponent's king as a shield, there is nothing that black can do anymore. White is going to promote to a queen, win the rook, and very simply win the game.
